We introduce a novel approach to represent the human mind's structure as a function network, where mental functions serve as the connections. Our method involves extracting mental functions by analyzing the brain's interconnected neural systems using advanced brain imaging techniques. The principles of correlation and quantum mechanics provide the foundation for understanding the relationship between mental functions and the brain's structure, leading to the development of a comprehensive mind model with all interconnected functions. This model offers a more accurate depiction of the mind's complexity and dynamics.

The classical Segal-Bargmann transform's properties have been expanded to functions with values in the Clifford algebra Rn^n, a mathematical structure that includes quaternions and complex numbers. In this context, a novel complexification of Rn is proposed, which enables the use of Clifford algebra-valued test functions and leads to the establishment of two key theorets: a modified Taylor isomorphism and a generalized Segal-Bargmann transform. These findings have far-reaching implications in mathematical physics and Clifford analysis.

We are focusing on the over-parameterization of the standard Gaussian process in its finite-dimensional version. Given a Gaussian field with a known covariance function, our goal is to determine the conditional distribution of a new sample given a Gaussian field sample on a specific grid. Our findings indicate that the conditional distribution exists and is unique up to measure-zero sets. Additionally, we discovered that the conditional distribution is highly sensitive to the sample path.

A recent study by the authors involved setting up a network of sensors on the ground and another above the Antarctic ice sheet to monitor the cosmic ray shower signals. To connect these two sets of sensors, which were located at different heights, we utilized the unique properties of short-wave radio waves. Due to the ionospheric reflection, short-wave signals can be transmitted over long distances, enabling the linkage of sensors situated on the ground and in the air. Short-wave waves have a frequency of around 3-30 MHz, corresponding to wavelengths of 100-10 m. This property makes them suitable for linking the sensors, which were operating in a frequency range of 2.5-3 MHz.

The next major experiment in long-baseline neutrino physics, Dynamic Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), will be a defining project for the future of the field. By utilizing a 40 kiloton liquid argon detector located 3,850 kilometers away from the Fermilab Site, DUNE will have the capability to study a variety of critical topics in neutrino science, including the measurement of the CP-violating phase $\phi_{CP}$, matter-antimatter asymmetry, neutrino mass hierarchy, and the octant of the largest neutrino mixing angle $\theta_{23}$. Furthermore, DUNE will have the power to study supernovae and dark matter. With its advanced capabilities, DUNE will be at the forefront of the subfield of neutrino physics, with the potential to make groundbreaking discoveries.

We've developed a model for identifying top quark decays in high-energy collisions between protons at the Large Hadron Collider. The model utilizes a combination of fully-convolutional and attention-based neural networks to process information from final-state particles. Our analysis of the model's performance revealed the significance of various parameters, including the transverse momentum of particles, with a focus on particles moving in the direction of the top quark.

This document establishes the theoretical framework and precise definitions for key concepts including Virtual Organizations, Service Requests, Service Combinations, Service Composition, Made-For, Made-From, Enhance, and Refined. It further develops a formal model of Virtual Organizations and proposes a formal enhancement of VOs through the refinement of their constituent services. The document concludes by demonstrating how Made-for, Made-from, and enhance relationships can be expressed using refined services and their corresponding make relationships.

The standard Deep Q-Network (DQN) algorithm, a widely used method in Reinforcement Learning, employs a technique called replay buffer to store past transitions and sample from it during training. Although this was initially used to stabilize learning, it also aids in balancing state distribution, an aspect often overlooked in research. A new variant called VarDQN, called here Variance Decrease DQN, modifies the traditional DQN approach by prioritizing experiences characterized by high reward and low uncertainty. This leads to an accelerated rate of improvement in the Q-function, ultimately enhancing the final performance of the DQN model.

The generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation is a widely used method in physics for solving complex many-body problems. However, a superior and more efficient method, the superbosonization equation, has been overlooked. In this study, we demonstrate that these two approaches are actually equivalent, with the superiority of the superbosonization equation becoming evident when applied to specific many-body problems.

Motion recognition is a critical area of study, particularly in fields such as sports analytics, robotics, and gesture identification. The success of deep learning models heavily relies on their ability to extract meaningful information from data. To address this challenge, a novel method, MoDeRNN, has been developed to enhance the understanding of motion data by leveraging recurrent neural networks. The MoDeRNN approach utilizes a novel motion layer that breaks down motion data into spatial and temporal components, enabling the extraction of detailed motion insights. The effectiveness of MoDeRNN has been demonstrated through its superior performance in predicting motion data and its ability to provide motion insights for downstream tasks such as prediction and analysis.

We introduce Josephine, a language feature that integrates JavaScript and Rust, 
aiming to combine the safety advantages of Rust with the extensibility of 
JavaScript. Josephine allows for secure management of the lifetimes of Rust data 
within the context of the JavaScript environment.

Theoretical research has demonstrated that neutrinoless double-beta decay can be observed at high-energy colliders through the emission of a characteristic, wide-angle pair of electrons. This process is influenced by neutrino mass eigenstates, which can interfere with each other, resulting in a shift in the decay's differential rate distribution. Our study presents a new method for estimating the sensitivity of a proposed high-energy collider to this phenomenon. This includes calculating the sensitivity to individual neutrino mass states, which can be derived directly from their contributions to the decay. Our findings indicate that the proposed Compact Muon Collider, a modification of the LHC, can achieve the highest sensitivity to this decay among colliders thus far. This is equivalent to an effective neutrino mass of approximately 10 eV, surpassing previous limits by a factor of 3.5.

This paper introduces a novel transmission method for binary polar codes, called the polar list decoding subcode, which enhances traditional polar list decoding by listing only the subcode that maximizes channel capacity. We demonstrate in the paper that this subcode can be further decomposed into multiple smaller subcodes with varying partial capacities, and polar codes of different lengths within each subcode, effectively transforming them into weaker symmetric and binary erasure channels. A new transmission scheme based on this decomposition is proposed, where a channel input sequence is divided among multiple subcodes, and a novel polar list decoding process is developed to determine the most likely subcode, followed by decoding each subcode separately. Simulation results show that the proposed scheme significantly outperforms conventional polar list decoding in the finite random coding regime, and the subcode selection process can achieve a coding diversity gain of up to m, where m represents the total number of subcodes.

When merging multiple images of a celestial object, such as a galaxy, to enhance their quality, it's crucial to consider the total point spread function of the combined images. We have developed an exact method for calculating the point spread function of merged images, which can be particularly useful to study the structure of galaxies. We have also developed an efficient approach to calculate these point spread functions numerically, even for images with high resolution. We have tested this method using two galaxies as examples and found that it can accurately model the pixel covariance of stacked galaxy images. We have further developed a novel technique to estimate the point spread function of a single image, which can be utilized for stacking galaxy images.

We utilize the concept of an energy-driven crack to investigate the fracture characteristics of crystalline materials. Our research reveals that the fracture strength of an imperfect crystal with dislocations is significantly weaker than its perfect, dislocation-free counterpart. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the fracture strength of a crystal with dislocations is influenced by the density of dislocations and that, as the crack grows, this influence becomes even more pronounced. Interestingly, our study also reveals that the fracture surface of a material weakened by dislocations may exhibit a non-planar structure. Additionally, our research explores how the material's atomic bond energy and the energy required to break dislocations impact the material's fracture behavior. Lastly, our study investigates how the material's atomic structure and the energy required to break dislocations impact the material's fracture behavior.

We establish a stochastic differential equation linking the two-dimensional Gaussian free field with the SLE $n$ process, where the SLE curves form the boundary of a random domain, and the equation's driver is the total SLE curve.

Explicit estimates for the $L^\infty$ norm of the answer to the Navier-Stokes equations are derived using specially designed Fourier series operators, given the initial data is periodic and the solution has zero mean.

The escalating need for advanced computational power has sparked interest in the quantum computing field, with the promise of significant improvements in solving complex problems. However, the current state of quantum devices is still in the noisy intermediate scale quantum (NISQ) era, where the reliability of quantum algorithms remains a concern. To address this issue, we propose a quantum calculator designed to verify quantum computations in the NISQ era, capable of operating within the same time frame as the calculations it is verifying. Our proposed approach is demonstrated through its application in validating Grover's algorithm, the use of complex vectors in NISQ-era quantum devices, and the use of phase estimation to ensure the accuracy of quantum calculations.

The widespread adoption of the Internet of Things (IoT) has led to the creation of vast networks of interconnected devices, which hold immense potential for transforming the global economy. However, these benefits are hindered by the lack of a reliable and secure infrastructure capable of ensuring data integrity and trustworthiness. In an effort to address this issue, researchers have begun exploring the application of blockchain technology to IoT settings. This paper proposes a novel blockchain framework tailored for IoT environments, which integrates oracular services and advanced rule-based agreements to enhance security and operational efficiency. The framework is demonstrated through a real-world use-case in the food supply chain, where it effectively tracks the provenance of products, optimizes inventory management, and minimizes waste.

Generative models have been successfully used in computer vision to create realistic images by learning the statistical patterns of a given dataset. In a recent study, a novel approach was developed to generate realistic cell images by using neural networks to represent the images directly. The implicit neural representations learned by this approach encode a meaningful latent space, allowing for the analysis of cell shapes and their biological processes. Notably, shape descriptors derived from these representations correlated with known changes in biological mechanisms, such as cell division, providing valuable insights for future applications in the field of computational biology.

Print impairment refers to an individual's inability to receive print-based information, which is a common challenge for visually impaired individuals. To address this limitation, a document must be available in an accessible digital format, such as XML, to ensure that screen readers can effectively convey the document's content to visually impaired users. Unfortunately, many digital documents are not available in this format, which results in the exclusion of a significant number of visually impaired users from online content. This paper aims to highlight the importance of making digital content accessible to visually impaired individuals, and proposes the use of image-to-text conversion as a potential solution to bridge this gap.

The highly successful Transformer architecture has significantly advanced NLP, with pre-training/ fine-tuning methods achieving top-tier performance on numerous tasks. However, current pre-training techniques have limitations, with masked language modeling falling short on sentence-level tasks and exposing non-autoregressive training to data leakage. In contrast, our proposed model, XLNet, is an autoregressive pre-training method that overcomes these issues. By utilizing permutations for input, it allows for rich next-token predictions and more effective data exploitation. In experiments, our model surpasses previous results on numerous GLUE and SQuAD benchmarks, demonstrating its superior performance.

The study of exoplanet atmospheres through transit spectroscopy is a rapidly evolving field, but stellar activity poses a significant challenge to its development.  This work aims to provide a straightforward approach to understanding how low-resolution stellar features impact the analysis of transmission spectra.  It involves creating a statistical model of starlight that is blocked by a planet, and then uses this to calculate a star's spectrum that can be compared to the observed spectrum of an exoplanet.  This comparison can be used to determine the characteristics of an exoplanet's atmosphere.  This method can be used to determine the effects of certain types of stellar features on the observed spectrum, and can be used to develop a way to remove these features from the data.  This method is tested using data from the High Resolution Transmission Spectroscopy, and the results show that it can be used to remove certain types of stellar features from the data.  This method is particularly useful for planets with low-resolution spectra, and can be used to improve the accuracy of certain types of atmospheric analysis.

We develop a method to transform a complete Riemannian manifold into one with constant curvature through a singular conformal transformation, specifically for cases where the original manifold has a non-zero average curvature and no geometric obstructions to conformal flatness. The resulting manifold will be conformally equivalent to a simpler manifold with no geometric singularities, making it a subset of the latter. The validity of our method is proven for a broader class of manifolds and provides a generalization of a previously established theorem.

Our investigation into the swimming behavior of the centipede Scutigera coleoptrata in various fluid environments reveals that the animal employs a consistent and efficient locomotion pattern across a wide range of speeds, regardless of the surroundings. Our analysis of the data shows that the body undulation in this species is optimized for speed in free swimming conditions, but becomes less efficient in more viscous fluids. Notably, the water's surface tension significantly impacts the animal's performance in confined environments, causing a marked decline in locomotion efficiency. Our findings also indicate that the animal's body position and leg movement are significantly affected by the surface tension in confined environments, while remaining relatively unchanged in fully submerged conditions.

The study of Tsunami Hydrodynamics involves complex computational models, such as the Navier-Stokes equations, which are computationally intensive. This research explores the feasibility of using a simplified model to simulate Tsunami dynamics in a more computationally efficient manner. A series of tests using the OpenFOAM software and a grid-based method are conducted to assess the model's accuracy in different scenarios. A key test involves the interaction of a tsunami with a solid object, which is a challenging situation to model accurately. By analyzing the test results, a more efficient simulation approach is proposed, which could be applied to the study of Tsunamis resulting from Asteroid collisions.

Recent observations of the James Webb Space Telescope have revealed a previously unknown population of luminous galaxies at high redshifts. These galaxies, which are invisible in the optical spectrum, are being discovered in the mid-infrared and are believed to be a significant component of the cosmic star formation history. A new study aims to understand the properties of these hidden galaxies by analyzing a sample of 140 candidates detected in the mid-infrared but not in the near-infrared. By using photometric redshifts and cross-correlating with large optical surveys, the study found that the majority of these galaxies are located at redshifts greater than 3.5, with a mean redshift of 4.5. These galaxies are primarily found in the southern hemisphere and are predominantly located in the sparsely observed fields. By analyzing the spectroscopic data of a subset of these galaxies, the study found that their mid-infrared emission is dominated by thermal dust, which is consistent with starburst activity. These findings support the idea that these hidden galaxies are responsible for the missing star formation in the high-redshift universe.

This comparison is then applied to a seven-dimensional sphere and a rotating black hole in seven-dimensional spacetime.

Utilizing the recently released NOAA Extended Truncated Index, we examined the differential impact of various El Ni\~no/Southern Oscillation phenomena on global precipitation patterns, specifically in regions experiencing significant seasonal rainfall variability. Our analysis revealed that these phenomena manifest distinctly in their low and high precipitation regimes, with notable spatial and temporal differences. Notably, the phenomenon known as the Pacific High-Elevation Oscillation (PHOE) was found to be more pronounced in its low-precipitation state, with significant effects observed in regions such as the Mediterranean, East Asia, and the Amazon. Conversely, the phenomenon known as the Pacific Low-Elevation Oscillation (PLEO) was found to have notable effects in the Amazon and the Sahel region. These findings suggest that the relationship between ENSO and global precipitation is more complex than previously thought, with multiple pathways and interactions at play.

A method is developed to study non-affine growth using light scattering, enabling the investigation of internal structure in non-affine materials. By creating a hole within such a material, researchers can measure the scattered light intensity to map the deformation field, thus gaining insight into how the material behaves during growth. This technique is applied to a polymer gel with non-affine properties, and the results show that light can penetrate the gel effectively. Moreover, introducing a hole within the gel significantly boosts scattering, providing a clearer picture of deformation patterns. Using this approach, scientists measure the internal deformation field, revealing that the gel grows non-affinely near the hole.

In this study, we have developed a comprehensive single-species demographic model, taking into account the physiological age of individuals and the adverse impact of a contaminated environment. The three-dimensional model, expressed as a system of partial differential equations, describes the single-species population density in terms of three key factors: the density of non-reproductive individuals who are contamination-resistant, the density of reproductive individuals who are contamination-resistant, and the density of reproductive individuals who are contamination-susceptible. The solution to this model is analyzed, and we have derived a maximum sustainable yield (MSY) for the single species, along with the corresponding harvesting efforts and age at which to harvest. The model's outcomes are validated through three-dimensional and two-dimensional graphical representations. The findings of this study can be applied to the management of species in contaminated areas, such as the Hudson River and areas affected by the Chernobyl nuclear disaster.

Substructural logic's framework, rootedin the weakening and contraction properties, forms the basis of the proposed research framework. Our work specifically focuses on the reduction operator within this context. The research involves developing hypersequent calculi for a broad range of non-classical logics, including those with both additive and multiplicative forms of conjunction and disjunction. The studied systems, however, do not include contraction. The focus of our investigation lies in the concept of decidability, complexity, and the computational properties inherent to these systems. Our findings reveal the underlying complexity classes for the various decidable cases, with the systems' properties directly influencing the resulting complexity classes.

Intelligent classification systems are crucial for many applications, but they are limited by their fixed classification structures. Expanding these systems dynamically can greatly enhance their adaptability, yet conventional methods rely on taxonomic classification expansion, which is often impractical. In this study, we introduce a novel approach to classification expansion based on learning representations in hyperbolic space. Hyperbolic classification layers are designed to model complex classification structures more effectively than traditional Euclidean space. By utilizing graph neural networks, we can simultaneously expand classification layers and embed individual samples into hyperbolic space for accurate classification. Our method's efficacy is demonstrated through successful tests on real-world hierarchical classification datasets.

Our research examines how electric fields impact molecular interactions among molecular dimers, including hydrogen-bonded complexes, using the S66 dataset. We've discovered that the results from our quantum-based model align with experimental findings, especially for dimers that form hydrogen bonds, in both non-polar and polar solvents. We've also determined that the effects of electric fields on molecular interactions are primarily due to the induction of electric dipoles, a phenomenon that becomes more pronounced in dimers that form hydrogen bonds. Furthermore, we've identified that the effects of electric fields on molecular interactions are more significant at longer equilibrium distances, and that the effects are more pronounced in dimers that form hydrogen bonds. Our findings are consistent with experimental data, including those for hydrogen-bonded complexes, and we've also verified that the effects of electric fields on molecular interactions are more significant at longer equilibrium distances. Our research has also revealed that the effects of electric fields on molecular interactions are more significant in dimers that form hydrogen bonds, and that the effects are more significant at longer equilibrium distances. Our findings are consistent with experimental data, including those for hydrogen-bonded complexes, and we've also verified that the effects of electric fields on molecular interactions are more significant in dimers that form hydrogen bonds, and that the effects are more significant at longer equilibrium distances.

To fully capitalize on Industry 4.0's potential, it is crucial to effectively handle non-deterministic data, particularly in complex scheduling tasks. This study introduces a new approach to tackling non-deterministic data in Industry 4.0, specifically processing times, through the integration of non-deterministic transpositions of groups. This concept is then applied to develop a generalized scheduling model, which encompasses several well-known scheduling models as special cases. By transposing the job-shop scheduling model with uncertain processing times, we obtain a novel non-deterministic model, which, in a specific instance, reduces to the previously established non-deterministic job-shop scheduling model. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm to tackle a specific case of this new model, which involves determining an optimal schedule for two machines and an arbitrary number of jobs with non-deterministic processing times. This algorithm generates an entire set of possible schedules by considering all possible processing times, and we establish a polynomial-time method to identify an optimal schedule among these possibilities.

Significant progress has been made in developing metrics to measure the quality of cyber-physical systems, particularly in the context of safety assessment. A notable approach centers around a logical framework that quantifies robustness as a function of temporal observations, and has seen widespread application in systems like autonomous vehicles. However, this methodology has struggled to accommodate scenarios where sensors and actuators are involved, as well as situations where control inputs are determined by external factors. In this paper, we introduce an innovative perspective on robustness, rooted in the theory of Signal Temporal Logic (STL), which seamlessly integrates sensor data and control inputs into a unified framework. By doing so, we provide enhanced measures of system robustness, and facilitate comparisons between control strategies.

This study presents an analysis of physical objects' movement by integrating advanced sensor technology into investigative procedures. Accelerometers, compact and highly efficient, serve as pivotal tools for tracking an object's trajectory and recording data on its momentum and velocity. This study explores the implications of Newton's laws in a context where objects are treated as having mass, rather than light, substance. Emphasis is placed on the significance of mass as a fundamental property, rather than an optional feature. Additionally, this study examines the relationship between an object's mass and its movement, as well as the impact of external forces on object behavior.

Solving the nonlinear diffusion equation on the manifold surface can be computationally expensive, but a linear equation-based approximation offers more efficient alternatives. A previous study developed nonlinear approximations by incorporating the structure of the surface into the sampling process. This research extends those findings to manifolds of infinite extent, proving that they apply to the bounded manifold approximation method. Additionally, it introduces and validates novel nonlinear approximations tailored for Gaussian sample sets, which are frequently encountered in Monte Carlo simulations. These samples often arise in financial modeling and physical system analysis, such as the behavior of particles in the Brownian dynamics.

The sources in the 1.4 GHz All Sky Survey catalog, specifically those with radio flux under 0.3 mJy, were analyzed using the XCSAND tool to determine the mean surface brightness and effective angular radius by stacking. This was done for 1.8 million sources across 10 bins of angular dimension. Our findings indicate that the mean surface brightness of these sources increases with angular dimension, and sources with smaller angular dimensions tend to have higher surface brightness. This is attributed to the sources being extended objects, such as radio galaxies, where the observed point-like appearance is due to their small angular size. Additionally, we found that the mean surface brightness of the sources in question is comparable to that of a sample of compact radio galaxies, and we observed a trend where the sources' angular distribution changes with angular dimension, and this is also seen in a sample of radio galaxies.

Concealed Markov models, a refinement of the classical Markov model, are proposed as a data flow mechanism. They integrate the concept of internal states, which are hidden from observation, into a model's structure. The Markov chain, representing the model's behavior, is then used to describe its behavior on this hidden state space. A formal explanation of the model's behavior is given through the refinement of the monadic structure of the classical model's power monad. This approach allows for the representation of data flow that depends on both external and hidden states. Additionally, it is shown how data flow algorithms can be factorized into distinct components, one representing the data flow's logical structure and the other representing its dynamic behavior. This separation enables the development of a language that is independent of time.

In various fields, such as fluid dynamics and materials science, there is a significant interest in understanding the behavior of complex systems. A notable example is the representation of turbulent flows through consistent structures that capture essential non-local relationships. A statistical framework has been developed to capture these non-local effects in a mathematically rigorous way. This framework relies on the concept of conditional probability and demonstrates its utility in modeling diverse systems, such as turbulence and atomic structures. By using Stiefel manifolds, the statistical framework can be efficiently computed and applied to a range of systems. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to provide a unified and comprehensive description of non-local effects, which has significant implications for a range of fields.

We introduce a phenomenological model for flexible (or viscoelastic) scattering, incorporating the influence of flexural rigidity, which is particularly significant for stiffened membranes. Our approach derives parameters from the equilibrium static properties of the involved molecules. The scattering force is time-dependent, taking into account the scattering time and rigidity. We test the model using two scenarios: an elastic scattering event between a rigid and flexible plate, and the dynamics of two flexible plates with opposing viscoelastic properties. Scattering is elastic in the former inorganic-scattering scenario and inelastic in the latter organic-scattering scenario. Our findings demonstrate that ignoring flexural rigidity can lead to unphysical outcomes, such as excessive energy dissipation.

This study proposes a new approach to evaluating privacy risks in continuous location tracking. Our method involves defining a transformation of an adversary's knowledge state, under which the adversary's expectations regarding a user's location remain consistent. Building upon this foundation, we introduce the concept of conditional expectation-preserving relations and derive the associated privacy mechanisms. Additionally, we examine the characteristics of these mechanisms, including their continuity, monotonicity, and convexity. Furthermore, we investigate the optimal mechanisms in finite settings and their corresponding data release strategies.

The Point Cloud Library (PCL) is a widely used software library for processing 3D point clouds, and the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) algorithm is a well-known method for representing 3D geometry in the NDT framework. The NDT algorithm has been extensively used for 3D point cloud-to-point cloud registration and robot localization, but its performance is limited by its reliance on computationally intensive optimization methods. We propose a new method that leverages the strengths of the Transformer architecture to accelerate NDT-based localization. Our method, NDT-Transformer, utilizes the Transformer architecture to efficiently extract local and global features from point cloud data, enabling faster and more accurate localization. We evaluate the performance of NDT-Transformer on the KITTI benchmark and demonstrate its ability to outperform traditional NDT-based methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency.

The concept of functional connectivity in resting-state brain networks is widely accepted, but its application to binary classification models in neuroimaging has limitations. Our research aimed to develop a more reliable method for using functional connectivity in binary classification models. We utilized the Human Connectome Project dataset to create a more accurate and reliable model. By comparing the performance of Gaussian and Bernoulli distributions, we found that using a binary model significantly increased prediction precision, while using the Bernoulli distribution resulted in stronger functional connectivity and better predictions. Our findings suggest that binary models can be more effective in understanding brain structure and function.

In a beeping network, nodes can only detect when other nodes are transmitting but not who is sending the message. We investigate the Broadcast Complexity Naming problem, which involves creating a short protocol where each node can identify itself through a sequence of transmissions that forms a broadcast tree. We focus on minimizing the power consumption of nodes by defining two types of objectives: $\min\max$ and $\min\sum$, which seek to minimize the maximum and total power usage per node, respectively. We develop a protocol for $\min\max$ that works in any network and also provide a lower bound on the total power usage. Furthermore, our analysis shows that total power usage can be significantly higher than maximum power usage in some cases. We also examine the feasibility of achieving the optimal solution in polynomial time.

This research paper presents a groundbreaking approach to address the challenges associated with code-mixed texts, which pose difficulties for natural language processing due to their fluid and ever-changing nature. We introduce a novel transition point-based model that captures the dynamic shifts in language use, thereby providing a more accurate representation of code-mixed texts. Our model, grounded in a data-driven methodology, automatically detects and incorporates the subtle variations in language use, thereby outperforming existing approaches in both the realms of task-agnostic code-mixed representation and code-mixed classification. Our findings demonstrate that this innovative approach effectively captures the intricacies of code-mixed texts, thereby providing valuable insights for future research in multilingual NLP.

The impact of varying pressure on H$_{3}$S hydride superconductor's critical temperature and the effect of isotope substitution on it are investigated. The relationship between these factors and the macroscopic properties of the superconductor is explored, particularly in relation to its electronic density of states and the phonon electron coupling constant. The study reveals that H$_{3}$S hydride superconductor undergoes significant changes in its electronic structure and phonon modes under pressure, leading to a decrease in the gap energy and a significant change in the isotope influence coefficient. The pressure-induced decrease in the van Hove singularity's contribution to phonon electron coupling is found to be a key factor in the isotope influence coefficient's change, particularly at higher pressures.

In environments that change over time, such as those encountered by robots, it's crucial to adjust their motion planning accordingly. When a space becomes inaccessible due to dynamic changes, a robot motion planner must be able to update itself to avoid using that space. This paper presents a new method for efficiently integrating dynamic constraints into a robot motion planner, focusing on collision detection and removal from the planner's configuration space, specifically in the case of a convex moving object.

Visual relocalization is a crucial computer vision task that involves determining a camera's position and orientation given a current image and a map of the environment. Our proposed method combines machine learning-based image features with 3D surfel map representations to achieve highly accurate relocalization, even in situations where there is limited visibility or dynamic changes occur. The proposed deep learning-based feature extraction model trains directly on raw images, resulting in features that are both distinctive and resilient. Our experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in various challenging environments, including those with limited visibility and dynamic changes.

In multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) networks, a novel approach is proposed to optimize user selection and link adaptation. The objective is to maximize the sum of the minimum user rates, resulting in a complex optimization problem. To make this problem more tractable, it is reformulated as a group LASSO problem. By leveraging the sparsity-promoting properties of group LASSO, a group LASSO problem is derived, which can be efficiently solved using the proximal point method. To further enhance performance, an encoding technique is introduced, specifically tailored for the selected user groups. The proposed solution framework is evaluated through simulations, which demonstrate its effectiveness in adapting to user mobility and channel conditions.

We demonstrate that a particular group within the tropical semifield $\mathbb{T}$, specifically related to the logical functions of a tropical curve, is generated over a simpler structure that's composed of a finite number of elements from $\mathbb{T}$. Our approach relies on the observation that a specific subgroup within the tropical additive group, which forms the basis of our method, is generated by a finite number of elements, namely three. This result is achieved by reducing the general case to its most fundamental case, which involves a basic three-element generator. Furthermore, a related finding states that a particular subgroup within the tropical additive group, which corresponds to the kernel of a map from $\mathbb{T}$ to a finite field, is generated by just three elements.

This study examines the convergence of a stochastic iterative process, which alternates between solving a constrained convex problem and an unconstrained problem, to a deterministic algorithm known as the Q-procedure used in robust control. It aims to prove that the process converges to the quasiautomatic solution of the Q-procedure, which corresponds to a local minimum of the relevant q-function. While earlier research demonstrated convergence to q-fixed points under certain conditions, the current analysis achieves convergence under broader assumptions and without requiring the verification of specific identifiability criteria.

We've created a geometrically defined 3-loop and calculated a non-zero value for its associated Vassiliev invariant of order three. Our findings also reveal that this loop is not a member of a specific normal subgroup of the based fundamental group of the 2-skeleton of the E8 group, which, in turn, is equivalent to the based fundamental group of the complement of the Milnor fiber corresponding to the E8 group.

Using a spin-fluctuation approach, researchers have investigated the stability of nematic states in the superconducting material LiFeAs. They analyzed the irrelevance of s-d nematicity and discovered that the s-rm-s type nematic state, which is consistent with experimental results, is only marginally unstable. However, calculations show that the nematic state is not favored in the material, and that the system is more likely to enter a paramagnetic metal state. This conclusion is based on the findings that the nematic state is not supported by the calculated spin susceptibility and that the system is more likely to develop a weak ferromagnetic moment. These results are also in line with the experimental results of the material's pressure-dependent superconducting transition temperature and its response to uniaxial strain.

Our investigation of the 2HDM type-I model with a 100 GeV non-SM Higgs reveals that the FCNC coupling strength can reach $\sim 10^{-3} \times e/m_W$ without contradicting existing experimental data. Specifically, $\tau \to \mu \gamma$ and $\text{B}_s^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ processes impose the most stringent restrictions, allowing the model to evade current constraints. Furthermore, our analysis shows that direct searches at the LHC do not significantly impact the 2HDM parameter space. With anticipated improvements in measurement precision, the 2HDM will face enhanced constraints from $\text{B}_s^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ and electroweak precision tests, but the muon $(g-2)$ anomaly and future colliders' searches for heavy Higgs states will provide the most promising avenues for finding non-SM Higgs particles.

The application of neuroevolution to particle simulation programs has led to significant advancements in computational science, particularly in software engineering and physics research. By employing a two-tiered approach, where both internal algorithms and external particle behaviors are subject to evolution, researchers can achieve groundbreaking results in computational software and physics experiments. This methodology has been successfully demonstrated through a series of experiments involving neuroevolved algorithms for building complex structures, such as bridges and functional surfaces, without prior programming or explicit instruction.

We examine the robustness of anomalies in chiral gauge theories, particularly focusing on the role of the consistent anomaly. We explore its connection to the anomaly polynomial in higher-dimensional theories and how it translates to four-dimensional theories, where it's equivalent to a multiple of the gravitational anomaly when it has no gauge dependence. This equivalence holds true in scenarios where the anomaly can be eliminated through a redefinition of the fermion measure, resulting in a theory that's both consistent and free from gauge dependence. We then investigate the interplay between the consistent anomaly and the physical anomaly current, highlighting the distinct roles of the $\xi$- and $\eta$-terms. This distinction is crucial in understanding the transition from the consistent to the physical current and how the $\xi$-term's contribution to the physical current can be eliminated via a redefinition of the fermion measure. We also analyze the implications of the $\eta$-term's influence on the physical anomaly, particularly in scenarios where the anomaly's coefficient is non-zero. This distinction is further illustrated by examining the transition from the physical anomaly to the physical current and how the $\eta$-term's influence can be eliminated via a redefinition of the fermion measure. We then explore the implications of our findings on the understanding of the chiral anomaly and how it can be eliminated via a redefinition of the fermion measure. We examine the behavior of the Navier-Stokes equations at a specific point in time within a certain type of function space. Our analysis reveals that the continuity of solutions in this context relies on the ability of certain related spaces to be embedded within another important space. This embedding condition is not always met, which means the continuity may not hold under more general circumstances. Additionally, our findings also apply to the Stokes and Navier-Stokes equations when considering 2D periodic problems.

In certain antiferromagnetic dielectrics, the magnetic fields that control the frequency of magnons can be significantly impacted by both temperature and the magnetic field strength itself. As a result, a phenomenon occurs where magnons experience a shift in their resonance field when heated, which is amplified under specific experimental conditions. A method has been developed to study this phenomenon using a technique called frequency-modulation magnetic resonance, which allows for precise measurements of magnon properties. Our experiments revealed that in NdGaO3, the magnon resonance field increases by around 10% when the sample is heated to 300K, which represents a substantial increase compared to previous predictions. Our findings also show that the traditional theory used to explain magnon behavior is insufficient, and we have proposed a new theoretical framework to accurately account for these observations.

Loidreau's code-based cryptography system offers a dual-security system using 
either the secret key of a systematic generator for its code or the secret key of 
the original code with doubled length, created using the code's generator as 
a generalised Gaussian map. We challenge this system with two new attacks: 
first, we introduce a new approach to break the first security layer by altering 
the information-set of the code's generator, building on recent advancements. 
Second, we devise a novel attack on the second security layer, leveraging this 
alteration to recover the code's generator via the syndrome of the resulting code, 
effectively compromising the second security layer.

Language models pre-trained via masked language modeling (MLM) are widely used for multiple NLP tasks, but they are heavily dependent on the quality of their pre-training. Since word-level representations may be insufficient to capture the full meaning of words, a new pre-training approach is proposed. This approach leverages a dictionary of paired word and glossary terms to create additional training samples, enhancing the model's understanding of word relationships. By incorporating this word-term pairing into the MLM task, a Dict-BERT model is developed, showing superior performance in NLP tasks such as natural language inference, machine translation, and question answering. Furthermore, Dict-BERT demonstrates improved performance in downstream tasks like named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, and machine reading comprehension, with consistent gains across various datasets and methodologies.

The volume of certain minimal spanning subcomplexes and their continuity counterparts in various dimensions of simplicial and polytopal complexes are studied in this paper. These subcomplexes are minimal in terms of a specific expected weight function, which is a product of edge lengths, and are defined for different types of input data, including point clouds and filtered complexes. A major finding is that under specific conditions, these minimal subcomplexes exhibit a phase transition behavior, which is similar to that of a spanning tree. The expected volume of these minimal subcomplexes diverges for certain dimension inputs, and their lower and upper bounds are also studied.

In recent years, concerns over user data security have grown, particularly in service sectors like ride-hailing, healthcare, and student management systems. As a response, researchers have developed federated learning to balance data utility and protection. A key approach known as vertical federated learning, where different parties share specific user data, has received significant attention. We introduce the concept of pragmatic privacy assaults, specifically focusing on them in the context of the education sector. A pragmatic assault leverages external, publicly available information to enhance its effectiveness. We demonstrate that traditional privacy methods, such as vertical differential privacy and secure multi-party computation, are susceptible to these attacks. We also explore the difficulty of assessing model accuracy under these attacks and propose a novel attack type, called the cross-pragmatic assault, which utilizes information from multiple public sources. This type of attack can significantly compromise data protection and model utility in the education sector.

In a theoretical framework where color is not fully confined, a possible universe contains an anti-baryon in its most stable form. We investigate the decay of a B meson into a baryon and anti-baryon, specifically the processes $B^+ \to p \bar{p}$ and $B^0 \to \bar{p} \bar{n}$, using QCD light-cone sum principles. We develop new distribution amplitude models that account for the wave functions of proton and neutron, which are then used to calculate the relevant amplitudes for these decays. We also consider how charm quark contributions affect these processes, specifically through $D$ meson contributions in the channel $D^+ \to p \bar{p}$ and $D^0 \to \bar{p} \bar{n}$. We derive mathematical formulas for these decays using these principles and calculate their rates. We calculate the differential decay rates for $B^+ \to p \bar{p}$ and $B^0 \to \bar{p} \bar{n}$ and find that their values are significantly larger than previously thought. We find that $B^+ \to p \bar{p}$ has a branching ratio of $1.1 \times 10^{-7}$ and $B^0 \to \bar{p} \bar{n}$ has a branching ratio of $7.0 \times 10^{-8}

In the rapidly evolving interconnected urban environments, cybersecurity is a vital concern, and effective defense against potential attacks is a pressing priority.  The  Intelligent Defense Game (IDG) framework is a game-theoretic approach that evaluates a city's ability to defend against socio-cyber-physical attacks.  This study presents an advanced version of IDG, known as the Tactical Resource Administration (TRA) model, which simulates strategic decision-making in response to coordinated attacks on critical social targets.  The TRA model considers the efficient use of limited defense resources, accounting for the dynamic interplay between attackers and defenders.  By integrating real-world constraints and trade-offs, the TRA model enables accurate simulation and evaluation of defense strategies, ultimately aiding cities in selecting the most effective tactical resource allocation policies.

Investigating black holes and their counterparts, known as black stars, holds significant physical importance, particularly in a theoretical framework, where a first-order phase change occurs between them at the Hawking--Page temperature.  In this theoretical context, the black stars can be viewed as a form of infrared-modified photon gas, and the phase change between them represents a fundamental principle of thermal radiation transition.  A study of this phase change was conducted in a theoretical context, where the black holes and black stars were considered within a theoretical container.  In this theoretical context, the phase change was found to be analogous to a thermal phase change between two types of thermal radiation.  In addition, the phase change was found to be characterized by multiple critical points, and the study revealed a complex pattern of critical points and phase changes.  In this theoretical context, the phase changes and critical points were found to be interrelated in a manner that can be visualized as a three-dimensional landscape.

In the field of machine learning, data annotation is a costly process, and to mitigate this cost, researchers have developed methods to efficiently utilize imperfect labels. One such application is article ranking, which involves processing large volumes of text. This paper presents an enhanced version of the BNA noise label correction approach, which can be adapted to various group ranking tasks. The key innovation is a bag sampling technique that calculates the probability of sampling a bag of data based on its loss, ensuring that high-quality data is easily accessible. The enhanced approach, denoted as BNA-G, has been rigorously tested on multiple datasets, including the NYT and IMDB articles, and has demonstrated superior performance compared to the baseline BNA and other prominent noise label correction algorithms.

The widespread use of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in various applications is hindered by their reliance on large amounts of labeled data, which is often scarce. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed semi-supervised pseudo-labeling methods that utilize unlabeled data to enhance the training of GNNs. However, existing methods that apply pseudo-labeling to individual data points can lead to the incorporation of noisy labels, which negatively impact the performance of GNNs. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called G-Pseudo, which aims to improve the accuracy of pseudo-labeling by considering the relationships between unlabeled data points and their predicted labels. By modeling the pseudo-labeling process as a probabilistic graph, our method can identify the most reliable labels and eliminate noisy ones. Through comprehensive experiments on benchmark datasets, our proposed G-Pseudo approach demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods.

A recent experiment at CERN's PARCOUR linear accelerator, known as AWAKE, is investigating an innovative method of particle acceleration that utilizes a intense, short laser pulse to initiate the self-generated electromagnetic fields in a proton plasma. These electromagnetic fields evolve into an oscillating effect called betatron motion, which can potentially generate X-ray emissions that could be detected and analyzed using various x-ray spectrometers placed at the end of the LHCb detector. Our analysis of data from the AWAKE's second run revealed promising results, including localized enhancements in linear energy transfer (LET) and distinct patterns of radiation damage that could be identified in silver halide detectors and simulated tracks that match observed phenomena.

This study presents a differentially private learning of decision trees in a distributed setting, utilizing the frequency domain and Haar basis for data analysis. The proposed model, based on the Fourier DFT feature mapping, is designed to be efficient and scalable, and can be effectively trained using the gradient boosting algorithm. A key aspect of this work lies in the development of an expandable tree structure, and the application of noise reduction techniques, utilizing Gaussian noise and the Fast Fourier Transform for data feature extraction. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, and its ability to compete with state-of-the-art models, while also showing improved interpretability due to its decision tree format.

The R\'enyi distance $R_\alpha$ has emerged as a metric to quantify the dissimilarity between two probability distributions, particularly in the context of supervised and semi-supervised learning. This work proposes a method to minimize $R_\alpha$ by introducing a regularized, one-sided Bregman-based approximation. A Bregman proximal gradient algorithm is then developed to tackle this objective. This approach is versatile and can accommodate a wide range of distributions, supported by convergence proof under standard non-smooth optimization conditions. A comprehensive numerical analysis, involving both synthetic and real-world datasets, validates the proposed algorithm's effectiveness.

The temporal aspect of dependency networks, specifically chain event sets, can be
approached using a Bayesian graphical model. This can lead to an overly complex model
which may be mitigated through regularization. This study proposes a novel Bayesian model
selection method for determining the most likely network configuration, mapping the network
configuration to a sequence of random variables. This can be accomplished by utilizing Markov
Chain Monte Carlo to sample from the posterior distribution of the network configuration.

In the field of inverse problems, finding a solution with minimal norm is crucial for stability and is typically achieved using the classical Tikhonov regularization method. However, this approach requires knowledge of the noise level, and overestimating it can lead to a loss of the solution's key properties. A minimal norm approach that doesn't require this knowledge is proposed, and it is shown to converge to the solution with minimal norm as a parameter approaches zero. This new approach is equivalent to a dynamical system that can be solved numerically and is found to converge at a rate of $O(1/\log(1/\mu))$ towards the solution with minimal norm, where $\mu$ is the damping parameter.

Our investigation focuses on a unique type of robot that adheres to obstacles using a barrier-tapping mechanism. This mechanism, combined with friction, enables the robot to navigate and navigate the surface of the obstacle. As the robot moves, its body experiences periodic changes in dynamics, resulting in a phenomenon known as a bifurcation circle. Within this context, we have identified and analyzed the characteristics of a barrier-tapping mechanism known as the "flicker," which is a key factor in the robot's ability to navigate and navigate the surface of the obstacle. Furthermore, we have developed a mathematical model to simulate the robot's movement and to study the effects of the robot's size and shape on its movement. Our simulations have revealed that the barrier-tapping mechanism is a highly effective means of navigating and navigating the surface of the obstacle, and that the robot's size and shape can have a significant impact on its movement.

particularly when the impurities are spread out over a large area. We utilize a model 
where the impurities' effects are modulated by an energy source, and show how this 
affects the microwave conductivity and the superfluid density as functions of both 
energy and doping levels. When the impurities are wide, we observe that the superfluid 
density peaks at a specific doping level, and this peak shifts towards lower doping 
levels when the impurities' effects are modulated by higher energy levels. At higher 
energy levels, however, the superfluid density and microwave conductivity decrease, 
and the peak shifts towards higher temperature. When the impurities are narrow, the 
peak shifts towards higher temperature, and the superfluid density and microwave 
conductivity show significant changes. When the impurities are wide, the microwave 
conductivity decreases, and when the impurities are narrow, the microwave conductivity 
increases. Our model provides a framework for understanding the behavior of kinetic 
energy superconductors when doped and when exposed to various levels of contamination.

This article discusses a specific type of non-smooth mean curvature, known as the mean curvature from support functions. Various types of non-smooth curvature evolutions are explored, utilizing different solution methods such as viscosity solutions, regularized approximations, gamma-convergence discretizations, and more. These methods have been applied to non-smooth curvature evolutions, showcasing a rich diversity of approaches and techniques.

Planting in confined spaces such as balconies or windowsills can be challenging due to limited sunlight and space. Planting in pots allows for greater control over growing conditions, but it can be difficult to achieve desired plant characteristics like fuller foliage or vibrant flowers. To overcome this obstacle, we propose GrowSpace, a practical guide that teaches how to create distinct plant shapes through strategic pruning and styling techniques. We conducted an experiment by training a plant pruning policy on artificially created data, and then applied it to a real-world scenario by pruning a living bush on our balcony. The results show that GrowSpace effectively creates visually appealing plant designs, and we provide insights into the feasibility of expanding its application to more complex plants.

Our research introduces a novel method for constructing SLE curves on random quantum disks with conformal symmetry, offering a novel approach compared to the conventional chordal SLE defined through the radial SLE and Loewner evolution. A key advantage of our approach lies in its ability to simplify the verification of conformal invariance in SLE, as it explicitly exhibits the SLE's conformal symmetry derived from the underlying disk's conformal symmetry. Additionally, our method enables the development of new properties of SLE, including a straightforward derivation of the Senhambi equation and the identification of SLE as the conformal gluing of quantum disks, providing an explicit formula for SLE's natural sigma field.

The growing influence of image processing in the geoscience community necessitates
the establishment of a unified approach to processing and representing imaging data.
Currently, the geological image community lacks a standardized protocol, resulting in
a diverse array of file formats, processing methods, and representation techniques.
This paper outlines the objectives of an ongoing effort to streamline the geological
image format and processing workflow. The initiative aims to simplify and standardize
the geological image format and processing workflow.

We have calculated the contribution of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances to quark flavor specific observables in photoproduction of $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ from a nucleon target. Calculations were performed within the framework of a light-coning QCD model. The predicted differential cross sections for the observed processes align with experimental findings, particularly in the resonance mass range, and suggest a significant role for high-spin resonances. The calculated $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ asymmetries demonstrate a significant deviation from experimental data at higher energies, indicating a need for further research into non-resonant background processes.

This research details the process of preparing the MORPH-II dataset using the OpenCV library. MORCV is a widely-used, open-source Python-based package for image and video processing. The study leverages the framework and the pre-trained Cascade Classifier from MTRV to detect facial features. The open-source scripts utilized in this research are accessible on the corresponding author's GitHub repository.

We analyze the constraints on an ancient black hole population, created by curvaton decay, using data from gravitational wave detectors, cosmic microwave background observations, and gamma-ray telescopes. The constraints are derived from operating gamma-ray telescopes, not theoretical sensitivity limits. The study finds that the curvaton mass must be less than 10^-11 GeV, assuming a curvaton decay time of 10^17 seconds. This is a significant improvement on previous bounds derived from infrareddening observations. The constraints from gravitational waves and gamma-ray telescopes are independent of the Hubble constant, while those from cosmic microwave background observations are only valid for specific Hubble constant values. The research highlights the potential of gravitational wave and gamma-ray observations to provide new insights into the properties of ancient black holes and the curvaton field.

This study introduces a latent variable model to uncover hidden characteristics of high school graduates, including their academic aspirations, career ambitions, and personal aspirations. These unobserved traits are then used to develop a dynamic model that tracks the educational choices of individuals over time. This tracking encompasses decisions about college attendance, trade school enrollment, and work, and is analyzed using a multinomial logit model. The results indicate that each high school graduate possesses a unique set of latent variables influencing their educational choices, and that understanding these variables can provide valuable insights into individual decision-making. The study also finds that a high school graduate's educational trajectory is significantly impacted by their latent variables, and that a trade school attendee's tendency to return to school later in life varies depending on their initial trade school choice.

The potential for autonomous vehicles working together in groups, known as vehicle platoons, offers significant benefits such as enhanced safety, efficiency, and reduced fuel consumption. However, the challenge lies in ensuring smooth and effective platooning, especially when vehicles are not directly connected. This study proposes a novel self-organizing approach using a game-theoretic model to regulate platoons with automated vehicles and human-driven followers. The model's solution, based on mixed Nash Equilibrium, enables each participant to determine the optimal probability of linking up with the preceding vehicle, thereby facilitating platoon assembly. The results show that this approach can stabilize platoon formations and improve overall efficiency.

One significant drawback of using logistic regression for feature selection is the interaction effect, where seemingly insignificant features might appear important due to the presence of other features. We introduce a novel approach to mitigate this effect, utilizing F-tests to identify relevant features and remove those affected by the interaction effect. The proposed method is a two-step process: logistic regression is initially used to choose features, followed by an iterative refinement to eliminate interaction effects. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through various case studies, showcasing its superiority over traditional feature selection methods.

The intersection of Natural Language Processing and Journalism has long been of interest, with recent advances in language generation models enabling the exploration of new possibilities. A newly identified challenge in this area is the classification of generated text at the headline level, specifically for headlines that do not match the main title of their corresponding article. To address this problem, researchers have developed an approach using automatically created headlines, leveraging the effectiveness of pre-trained transformer models, specifically a modified version of BERT known as BERT-LC. A dataset consisting of 10,000 pairs of main and sub-headlines from a news domain was used to evaluate the performance of this approach, with results showing that it outperforms a baseline model by a significant margin, with an F1-score of 87.8%.

A polycrystalline arrangement of two types of magnets, with their spin orientations randomly arranged, presents an ideal setting for the emergence of a topological metal known as the chiral spin fluid.
Theoretical models have previously suggested that a specific type of spin arrangement in a uniform magnetic crystal can also host this metal, but these models are challenging to realize in a metal with a perfect crystal structure.
However, we demonstrate that this metal can be formed in a more accessible type of metal with a crystal structure that undergoes a specific type of distortion.
Our findings indicate that the surface of such a metal will display a unique type of magnetic behavior that can be easily manipulated, and we also show that the same type of metal can also be formed in a non-crystalline metal.
These findings have significant implications for the development of this metal in a wide range of materials, including those that are more easily synthesized and those that are more resistant to magnetic interference.

Achieving precise image reconstruction in large-scale radio interferometers is hindered by the need for precise gain calibration, which typically requires processing data computationally expensively. This research presents an innovative method for gain calibration that is suitable for large arrays with hundreds of thousands of elements. The proposed technique, leveraging the Fast Fourier Transform, reduces computation time to $O(N\log{N})$ and efficiently utilizes the properties of the Fourier transform to calibrate all sources simultaneously. This new approach is demonstrated through successful reconstruction of simulated images for the SKA PathFinder prototype, utilizing a fraction of the data, and is expected to be applicable to other large-scale radio telescopes.

A key concern in investment portfolio management is minimizing risk while optimizing returns. This study focuses on enhancing portfolio risk through the use of a diversified portfolio generator, a model inspired by the accuracy of deep learning. Leveraging historical data, the generator is designed to create synthetic data that can be used to develop a more resilient portfolio. Specifically, the research employs a denoising autoencoder-based conditional generative adversarial network to synthesize diversification data, which is then used to establish an optimal portfolio. The results demonstrate that the model successfully minimizes investment losses under adverse market conditions.

This study presents the results of a theoretical calculation of a crucial component, $A_{gq}(z,  N,  \mu^2)$, which influences the evolution of parton distribution functions within a QCD framework. Specifically, we have computed this function in a range of seven variables (four power, four loop orders) and derived its integral form, $\int dz A_{gq}(z,  N,  \mu^2)$, which plays a pivotal role in determining the transition matrix elements governing the behavior of these functions. This calculation is a significant advancement in the field, as it marks the first time $A_{gq}(z,  N,  \mu^2)$ has been computed in a range of seven variables (four power, four loop orders) and represents the last remaining element necessary to solve the problem of the running of the flavor number at $O(\alpha_s^4)$.

The rapid growth of gamma-ray source data has created a pressing need for efficient methods to process and analyze it.  Bayesian neural networks offer a promising solution, combining the power of deep learning with the reliability of uncertainty assessment.  In this research, a novel Bayesian neural network is developed for classifying Fermi-LAT detected quasars.  By training the network with 100 most probable radio galaxies and 100 probable quasars, the model achieves a high level of accuracy in quasar classification.  Moreover, the use of the Laplace approximation allows for the quantification of uncertainty in the model's predictions.  This approach demonstrates promising results, paving the way for the application of this method to real-time data analysis.

The rapid growth of social media has made it a vital source of information and entertainment for a diverse audience worldwide. However, a significant number of social media sites have accessibility issues, failing to cater to people with disabilities. As a result, disabled individuals face significant barriers to accessing online content, with only a small percentage able to access it independently. This paper explores the difficulties and potential challenges in creating accessible social media content and examines the potential benefits of universal design. It also highlights the need for further research and development in this area, including the creation of social media platforms that are accessible to all users.

The concept of tensor union of hypergraphs is introduced, followed by the development of sufficient conditions for identical edge per vertex and per vertex degree in the resulting tensor union hypergraphs, generated from given hypergraphs through a random process. We demonstrate that non-edge per vertex and non-vertex degree per information in tensor union hypergraphs can be utilized as encryption keys. We also explore the relationship between the spectrum of tensor union hypergraphs and the eigenvalue distribution of random vectors, ultimately deriving complete solutions for the spectrum of tensor union hypergraphs, formed from regular r-hypergraphs with uniform edge and vertex degrees.

India has long been a hub for successful space missions, including the Mangalyaan and Chandrayaan missions. To further its commitment to space exploration, the Indian Space Research Organisation is developing a cutting-edge space observatory called INSIST. This ambitious project aims to revolutionize the field of astronomy by providing high-resolution capabilities in both visible and near-infrared light. With a 1.2-meter mirror, the telescope will be able to capture detailed images of distant celestial objects and conduct high-resolution spectroscopy. By focusing on observing the universe within our own galaxy, the INSIST will be able to uncover new insights into star formation, the origins of planets, and the evolution of galaxies. This space observatory will greatly expand our understanding of the universe and open up a wealth of new research opportunities.

In clinical settings, cognitive assessments are typically measured using brief, limited scales. As a result, diagnosing dementia can be challenging due to the overlap between normal aging and early dementia indicators. To address this issue, a novel approach using natural cubic splines is proposed to create continuous cognitive scores from discrete scale readings. This method allows for a more accurate diagnosis and tracking of cognitive decline in Alzheimer's patients.

In the field of physics, identifying rare events with significant energy barriers is crucial. We have developed an enhanced approach to find these events by initially focusing on discovering transition pathways with the lowest energy barriers, which are often discovered using the nudged elastic band method. We then utilize the Landau-Khalatnikov equation to speed up event transitions, making it possible to uncover pathways that are typically inaccessible. Our method has been successfully tested in two model systems: the Ising system and the solvation dynamics of water molecules.

This paper offers L-infinity-approximations for the parabolic complex Monge-Ampere and Hessian equations within the C(omega)-class, along with the derivation of the corresponding parabolic solutions. We also establish the continuity of the maps in the C(omega)-class under uniform convergence for the corresponding parabolic solutions.

We've developed two enhanced typed lambda-calculi, each with specific type theories, that allow for the inclusion of a choice operator, resulting in the ability to represent specific subclasses of regular integer functions when the function domains and ranges are restricted to standard natural numbers. The two lambda-calculi incorporate different type theories, one based on Berstel's subword monoid and the other on the rationalised free monoid. Additionally, we've established corresponding term rewriting systems for the lambda-calculi and provided decision procedures for the respective inclusion problems.

This text describes a geometric stochastic method for solving forward Kolmogorov equations in one dimension that involves discontinuous functions, leading to a conditional probability flow with a specific operator structure. By applying a standard Stratonovich integral representation, a general solution is found, which is then converted into an equivalent Ito integral by using Ito's formula. This approach enables the determination of an effective drift term, thereby resolving the equation with a smooth drift term derived from jump source densities. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that this method can resolve a longstanding problem in physics concerning the Ito interpretation of Newton's equation with a discontinuous force.

A standard frame is a type of ordered structure, specifically an ordered set of bits that can be combined and managed through two key principles: de Morgan laws and the absorption principles. Within the context of groups, the frame of all subnormal series forms a standard frame, which we explore by introducing concepts like prime subnormal series, the standard space of a group, and the continuous maps within this framework. Our investigation also extends to the management of subgroups within the given frame by introducing the management frame of a group, which we explore by introducing concepts like prime management series, the standard space of the management series, and the continuous maps within this framework.

This study introduces a novel task, cross-domain text-to-SQL, which involves
identifying the database to query from given text, and then generating a SQL
query. The task aims to enhance text understanding by incorporating database
selection, thereby providing additional textual and structural cues. We propose
a unified framework, UniCode, to tackle both the database selection and text-to-SQL
tasks. The framework employs code-generation to produce SQL queries and uses an
embedded code tree to facilitate text parsing and extract database information.
Experimental results indicate that our approach is effective and that the
auxiliary code selection task benefits the text-to-SQL process.

This study presents an innovative data-driven risk-averse model predictive control (Dr-MPC) approach for secure multi-robot navigation within crowded environments. The proposed method integrates real-time sensor data with dynamic obstacle information to forecast potential threats and adjust navigation paths accordingly. A novel cost function is designed to minimize theMiR, a specific risk metric, by leveraging the covariance matrix of the state vector. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through a simulation of a multi-robot navigation scenario, which yields superior performance in terms of mission success rates, energy consumption, and computational efficiency compared to model-based and stochastic methods.
